Prim's algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree of a connected, weighted graph [MATH: G.] It follows a so-called greedy approach by starting from an arbitrary vertex and expanding the tree by adding the smallest edge that connects a visited vertex to an unvisited vertex. It is widely used in network design, constructing road systems, and optimizing cable connections.

Content:
The steps for Prim's algorithm are as follows:

Content:
- Step 1: Initialize a tree [MATH: T] consisting of a starting vertex [MATH: v] of [MATH: G.]
- Step 2: While not all vertices are in [MATH: T,] find the shortest edge [MATH: u - w] such that [MATH: u] is already in [MATH: T] and [MATH: w] is not.
- Step 3: Add vertex [MATH: w] and edge [MATH: u - w] to tree [MATH: T.]
- Step 4: Repeat this process until all vertices are included in [MATH: T.]

Content:
We can express Prim's algorithm using pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simplified, programming language-independent way of describing an algorithm. It uses a mix of natural language and programming concepts, helping programmers to plan and visualize code logic without focusing on syntax.

Content:
The pseudocode for Prim's algorithm is as follows.

Content:
> Initialize a tree T consisting of a starting vertex v of G
>
> while (not all vertices added to T):
>
> Find the shortest edge u-w of G such that
> (u in T) and (w not in T)
>

> Find the shortest edge u-w of G such that
> (u in T) and (w not in T)
